The tool has an elongated straight rail with a flat lower face that rests on the front face of a cabinet door or drawer front. A straight longitudinal slot runs through the rail. Distance marks are printed along the upper face beside the slot.

A fixed fence is attached at the first end of the rail. The fence extends downward from the lower face and bears against one straight edge of the workpiece. The fence is perpendicular to the rail, so the rail extends inward across the workpiece when the fence bears against the edge. A removable spacer plate can be fitted between the fence and the workpiece edge. The spacer plate has parallel opposite faces and changes the setback of every guided hole by its thickness without changing the separation between the holes.

Two separate guide carriages sit on the upper face of the rail. Each carriage has a lower key that passes into the longitudinal slot, and the key prevents the carriage from rotating while allowing it to slide along the slot. Each carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing with a vertical bore. The bore passes completely through the carriage and aligns with an opening through the slot so a drill bit can reach the workpiece. The two bushing axes are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face of the rail.

Each carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail. A threaded shank of the knob passes through the carriage and the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail. Turning the knob draws the shoe toward the carriage and clamps the rail between the carriage and the shoe. Loosening the knob allows the carriage to slide. The first carriage has a pointer aligned with its bushing axis and readable against the distance marks. The second carriage has its own pointer aligned with its bushing axis. The difference between the two pointer readings is therefore the center-to-center hole spacing.

The rail has a transverse center index at its midpoint. A shallow V-shaped sight notch is formed in the second end of the rail and aligned with the center index. The user can align the center index and the sight notch with a pencil centerline on the workpiece before tightening both carriage knobs. The fence controls setback from the workpiece edge, while the two pointer readings control hole separation and the position of the pair relative to the centerline.

The fence is reversible. It is secured to the first end of the rail by two screws received in two corresponding holes. Removing the screws, turning the fence over, and reinstalling the screws moves the downwardly projecting part of the fence from one longitudinal side of the rail to the opposite longitudinal side. This lets the same marked upper face be used when the tool is referenced from either an upper edge or a lower edge of a workpiece.

To use the tool, the user selects the desired hole spacing, loosens both clamp knobs, slides the carriages until their pointer readings have the desired difference and are centered about the transverse center index, and tightens the knobs. The user places the lower face on the workpiece, presses the fence or the installed spacer plate against the selected workpiece edge, aligns the sight notch and center index with the pencil centerline, and drills through both bushings. The tool is then lifted away. No part remains attached to the workpiece.

The rail, fence, carriage bodies, shoes, spacer plate, pointers, and knobs may be made from rigid polymer or metal. The drill bushings are replaceable wear parts and are made from hardened metal. The tool has no motor, battery, electronic sensor, or network connection.

input.content:
Mounting a pull on a cabinet door or a drawer front requires two holes that satisfy three separate conditions at once. The two holes must lie at a common setback from a straight edge of the workpiece, they must be separated by the center-to-center spacing of the particular pull being installed, and the pair must sit symmetrically about a chosen centerline of the workpiece. A hole that is correct in one of these three respects and wrong in another still spoils a finished panel, and a panel that has been drilled cannot be corrected by moving the hole.

Laying the holes out by hand with a rule and a square requires the installer to compute and mark two positions for every panel, to transfer each mark accurately, and then to start a drill bit exactly on a pencil intersection on a hard and often prefinished surface. Small errors in measuring, in marking, and in bit wander accumulate independently on each of the two holes, so the pair can be out of square with the edge even when each individual measurement was made carefully. Repeating the layout on every door and drawer front of a run multiplies both the labor and the opportunities for error.

Simple drilling guides reduce part of this burden by presenting a hardened bushing that both positions the bit and keeps it perpendicular to the surface. A guide of that kind still leaves the installer to establish where the guide itself is placed on the panel, and a guide that fixes the two bushings at a single separation serves only one pull pattern. Adjustable arrangements in which a scale is read once and a second hole is measured from the first reintroduce the accumulation of error that the guide was meant to remove, because an error in setting the single reading displaces both holes and an error in transferring the spacing displaces only one of them.

A further difficulty arises from the direction in which the workpiece is referenced. A pull on an upper cabinet door is commonly located from the lower edge of the door, while a pull on a drawer front or a base cabinet door is commonly located from the upper edge or from a stile edge on the opposite side. A jig whose edge fence projects from one longitudinal side of its body can be referenced from the opposite edge only by turning the whole jig over, which puts the marked and readable face of the jig against the panel where it cannot be seen, or by printing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which invites the installer to read the wrong scale. Neither expedient is satisfactory in the field, where the installer moves repeatedly between doors and drawer fronts on the same run of cabinets.

Powered and electronically assisted layout systems can measure and record positions, but they add cost, require charging or batteries, and are unnecessary for an operation whose entire geometry is fixed by one straight edge, one centerline, and one spacing dimension.

No prior art references were supplied with this application, and accordingly no publication is cited or characterized in this Background.

A drilling jig is disclosed that locates and guides both holes of a cabinet pull pattern in a single placement of a hand tool, without any powered measuring system.

The jig includes an elongated straight rail having a flat lower face that rests on the front face of a cabinet door or drawer front, an upper face, and a straight longitudinal slot extending through the rail from the upper face to the lower face. Distance marks are carried on the upper face alongside the longitudinal slot.

A fence is secured to a first end of the rail by two screws received in two corresponding holes. The fence has a portion that projects below the lower face and bears against a straight edge of the workpiece, and the fence is perpendicular to the rail so that the rail extends inward across the workpiece while the projecting portion bears against the edge. The fence is reversible. Removing the two screws, turning the fence over, and reinstalling the two screws moves the projecting portion from one longitudinal side of the rail to the opposite longitudinal side, while the marked upper face continues to face away from the workpiece. The same face of the rail, carrying the same distance marks reading in the same direction, is therefore used whether the tool is referenced from an upper edge or a lower edge of the workpiece, and the installer never has to read a second scale or work from an inverted tool.

Two separate guide carriages are seated on the upper face of the rail. Each guide carriage has a lower key that passes into the longitudinal slot, and the key prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot. Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing having a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot, so that a drill bit passed through the bore reaches the workpiece. The two bores are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face of the rail.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail. A threaded shank of the clamp knob passes through the guide carriage and the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail. Turning the clamp knob draws the clamping shoe toward the guide carriage and clamps the rail between the guide carriage and the clamping shoe. Loosening the clamp knob allows the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot.

The first guide carriage carries a first pointer aligned with the axis of its bore and readable against the distance marks, and the second guide carriage carries a second pointer aligned with the axis of its bore and readable against the distance marks. Each hole of the pair is therefore set by its own reading taken directly from the same scale, and the difference between the two pointer readings is the center-to-center hole spacing. An error made in setting one guide carriage does not propagate into the position of the other.

The rail has a transverse center index at its midpoint, and a shallow V-shaped sight notch is formed in a second end of the rail and aligned with the transverse center index. The transverse center index and the sight notch are aligned with a centerline marked on the workpiece before both clamp knobs are tightened, so that the pair of guided holes is placed symmetrically about the centerline. The fence controls the setback of the holes from the straight edge of the workpiece, while the two pointer readings control the hole separation and the position of the pair relative to the centerline. These three settings are made against three separate features of the jig and do not interfere with one another.

A removable spacer plate having parallel opposite faces may be fitted between the fence and the straight edge of the workpiece. The spacer plate changes the setback of every guided hole by its thickness without changing the separation between the holes, so that a second setback can be obtained without disturbing a spacing setting that has already been made.

In use, the installer selects the desired hole spacing, loosens both clamp knobs, slides the guide carriages until the pointer readings differ by the desired spacing and are centered about the transverse center index, tightens both clamp knobs, places the flat lower face on the workpiece with the fence or the installed spacer plate pressed against the selected edge, aligns the sight notch and the transverse center index with the centerline, and drills through both drill bushings. The jig is then lifted away, and no part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece.

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 5). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed, engraved, or otherwise permanently applied there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 5, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 may be retained between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 by the pressure of the user's hand as the jig is held against the workpiece 90, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are separately seated on the upper face 12 of the rail 10. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The construction of the first guide carriage 50 is shown in the transverse section of FIG. 3, and the second guide carriage 70 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 and a key 52 that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54. The drill bushing 54 has a bore 56 that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore 56 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore 56 has been enlarged by use, or whose bore 56 is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 lies below the lower face 14 and is thin enough that the lower face 14 continues to rest on the front face of the workpiece 90 with the clamping shoe 60 received within the recess formed by the pull hardware clearance, or the clamping shoe 60 is set into a shallow relief of the lower face 14, so that the flat lower face 14 seats on the front face of the workpiece 90.

Referring to FIG. 2, the first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

The rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

The drill bushing 54 has a bore 56 that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore 56 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore 56 has been enlarged by use, or whose bore 56 is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 lies below the lower face 14 and is thin enough that the lower face 14 continues to rest on the front face of the workpiece 90 with the clamping shoe 60 received within the recess formed by the pull hardware clearance, or the clamping shoe 60 is set into a shallow relief of the lower face 14, so that the flat lower face 14 seats on the front face of the workpiece 90.

Referring to FIG. 2, the first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

The rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 may be retained between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 by the pressure of the user's hand as the jig is held against the workpiece 90, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are separately seated on the upper face 12 of the rail 10. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The construction of the first guide carriage 50 is shown in the transverse section of FIG. 3, and the second guide carriage 70 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 and a key 52 that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54. The drill bushing 54 has a bore 56 that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore 56 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore 56 has been enlarged by use, or whose bore 56 is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 lies below the lower face 14 and is thin enough that the lower face 14 continues to rest on the front face of the workpiece 90 with the clamping shoe 60 received within the recess formed by the pull hardware clearance, or the clamping shoe 60 is set into a shallow relief of the lower face 14, so that the flat lower face 14 seats on the front face of the workpiece 90.

Referring to FIG. 2, the first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

The rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the bore 56 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the bore 56 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 lies below the lower face 14 and is thin enough that the lower face 14 continues to rest on the front face of the workpiece 90 with the clamping shoe 60 received within the recess formed by the pull hardware clearance, or the clamping shoe 60 is set into a shallow relief of the lower face 14, so that the flat lower face 14 seats on the front face of the workpiece 90.

Referring to FIG. 2, the first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

The rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 5). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed, engraved, or otherwise permanently applied there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 5, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 may be retained between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 by the pressure of the user's hand as the jig is held against the workpiece 90, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54. The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16.

The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

The rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

input.content: A hand drilling jig locates and guides both mounting holes of a cabinet pull in one placement on a door or drawer front. An elongated rail has a flat lower face, an upper face carrying distance marks, and a longitudinal slot. A fence at a first end of the rail is held by two screws in two mounting holes and has a portion projecting below the lower face that bears against a straight edge of the workpiece; removing the screws, inverting the fence, and reinstalling them moves that portion to the opposite longitudinal side of the rail while the marked upper face still faces the user, so one scale serves an upper or a lower reference edge. Two separate guide carriages seat on the upper face, each with a key in the slot that blocks rotation while allowing sliding, a hardened drill bushing whose bore registers with the slot, and a clamp knob whose shank reaches a clamping shoe below the rail. Each carriage carries a pointer aligned with its bore axis, so the difference between the two readings is the hole spacing. A transverse center index at the rail midpoint and an aligned V-shaped sight notch at the second end register the pair on a marked centerline, and a removable spacer plate at the fence changes setback without changing spacing.

A fence at a first end of the rail is held by two screws in two mounting holes and has a portion projecting below the lower face that bears against a straight edge of the workpiece; removing the screws, inverting the fence, and reinstalling them moves that portion to the opposite longitudinal side of the rail while the marked upper face still faces the user, so one scale serves an upper or a lower reference edge. Two separate guide carriages seat on the upper face, each with a key in the slot that blocks rotation while allowing sliding, a hardened drill bushing whose bore registers with the slot, and a clamp knob whose shank reaches a clamping shoe below the rail. Each carriage carries a pointer aligned with its bore axis, so the difference between the two readings is the hole spacing. A transverse center index at the rail midpoint and an aligned V-shaped sight notch at the second end register the pair on a marked centerline, and a removable spacer plate at the fence changes setback without changing spacing.

+A hand drilling jig locates and guides both mounting holes of a cabinet pull in one placement. An elongated rail has a flat lower face, an upper face carrying distance marks, and a longitudinal slot. A fence held at a first end by two screws has a portion projecting below the lower face that bears against a workpiece edge; removing the screws, inverting the fence, and reinstalling them moves that portion to the opposite longitudinal side while the marked face still faces the user. Two separate guide carriages seat on the upper face, each having a key in the slot that blocks rotation while allowing sliding, a drill bushing registering with the slot, a clamp knob whose shank reaches a clamping shoe below the rail, and a pointer aligned with its bore axis. A transverse center index and an aligned sight notch register the pair on a marked centerline.
