content.content:
1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.
2	
3	Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 5). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed, engraved, or otherwise permanently applied there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.
4	
5	The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.
6	
7	A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.
8	
9	Referring to FIG. 5, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.
10	
11	The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.
12	
13	A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 may be retained between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 by the pressure of the user's hand as the jig is held against the workpiece 90, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.
14	
15	Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are separately seated on the upper face 12 of the rail 10. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.
16	
17	The construction of the first guide carriage 50 is shown in the transverse section of FIG. 3, and the second guide carriage 70 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 and a key 52 that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.
18	
19	Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54. The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.
20	
21	The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.
22	
23	Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and spans the longitudinal slot 16, so that it bears against the lower face 14 on each side of the longitudinal slot 16 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened and travels with the guide carriage along the rail 10 when the clamp knob 58 is loosened.
24	
25	Referring to FIG. 2, the first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.
26	
27	Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.
28	
29	The rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.
30	
31	The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.
32	
33	In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.
34	
35	The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.
36	
37	When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.
38	
39	The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.
40	
41	The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.
42	
43	The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.
44

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 5). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed, engraved, or otherwise permanently applied there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 5, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 may be retained between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 by the pressure of the user's hand as the jig is held against the workpiece 90, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are separately seated on the upper face 12 of the rail 10. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The construction of the first guide carriage 50 is shown in the transverse section of FIG. 3, and the second guide carriage 70 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 and a key 52 that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54. The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.

The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 5). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed, engraved, or otherwise permanently applied there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 5, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 may be retained between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 by the pressure of the user's hand as the jig is held against the workpiece 90, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The construction of the first guide carriage 50 is shown in the longitudinal section of FIG. 3, and the second guide carriage 70 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key 52 that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54. The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and spans the longitudinal slot 16, so that it bears against the lower face 14 on each side of the longitudinal slot 16 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened and travels with the guide carriage along the rail 10 when the clamp knob 58 is loosened.

Referring to FIG. 2, the first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is a discrete index feature, such as a fine line or a tapered tip, that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

The rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the upper face 12 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, the apex of the sight notch 26 lying on the same transverse position along the rail 10 as the transverse center index 24. The sight notch 26 opens through the end edge of the rail 10, so that a pencil centerline 94 drawn on the front face of the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 and at the transverse center index 24 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed, engraved, cast, or molded features. The first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 may be formed integrally with the bodies of the respective guide carriages or attached to them as separate pieces.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

## View
Perspective view of the assembled drilling jig resting on a workpiece, seen from above and slightly to one side, so that the top of the jig and the near edge of the panel are both visible. Line work is drawn in plain black outline on white, entirely inside the drawing area and clear of the sheet margins.

## Structures and relationships

Workpiece 90: a flat rectangular panel drawn in perspective, lying with its front face upward and occupying most of the drawing area. The panel is drawn as a thin slab so that its thickness is visible along the near side. The straight near-side boundary of the panel is the workpiece edge 92.

Rail 10: a long straight bar of rectangular cross section lying flat on the front face of the panel. The rail runs from the near edge of the panel inward across the panel, at a right angle to the workpiece edge 92, and stops well short of the far boundary of the panel. Its flat underside is in contact with the front face of the panel along its whole length.

Longitudinal slot 16: a narrow straight through slot in the rail, running lengthwise along the middle of the rail's top face, open at the top face and stopping short of both ends of the rail. The slot is drawn as an elongated opening with rounded ends and is shown as an opening through the bar.

Distance marks 18: a row of short transverse tick marks on the top face of the rail, running along one side of the longitudinal slot 16, parallel to the slot and evenly spaced along most of the rail's length. The ticks are plain short strokes and carry no text.

Fence 30: a flat plate fitted across the end of the rail that lies at the near edge of the panel. The plate lies against the rail and extends sideways past one long side of the rail. From that extension a flange descends below the level of the rail's underside and stands against the near-side thickness of the panel. Two small round fastener heads are shown on the plate.

## View
Enlarged longitudinal sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2, the cutting plane standing vertically and running lengthwise along the middle of the rail through the first guide carriage, seen in the direction of the arrows of FIG. 2, so that the end of the rail carrying the fence lies to the left. Cut surfaces carry section hatching. Plain black outline on white, all line work well inside the drawing area.

## Structures and relationships

The rail appears in longitudinal section as a long horizontal slab spanning most of the width of the drawing area. Upper face 12 is its straight top boundary and lower face 14 its straight bottom boundary, the two parallel to one another.

Longitudinal slot 16: the cutting plane runs along the open slot, so the middle region of the slab is not cut material. That region is a plain unhatched band bounded above by the upper face 12 and below by the lower face 14, representing the far side wall of the slot seen beyond the cutting plane. Section hatching appears only in the two end portions of the slab, left and right of the band, where rail material closes the ends of the slot.

First guide carriage 50: a rectangular body seated on the upper face 12 above the band, drawn in section with hatching, its flat underside in contact with the upper face 12.

Key 52: a rib of that same hatched body depending from its underside into the band, filling part of the depth of the band and stopping above the level of the lower face 14, its left and right faces drawn as straight vertical lines.

Drill bushing 54: a cylindrical sleeve set vertically through the left part of the first guide carriage 50, drawn in section as two narrow hatched walls separated by an open bore, its outline distinct from the body outline so that it reads as a separate piece. The bore is open at the top of the first guide carriage 50, runs straight down through the key 52 and through the band, and is perpendicular to the lower face 14.

Clamp knob 58: a knurled head above the right part of the first guide carriage 50, spaced along the rail from the drill bushing 54, with a straight stem descending from it through the first guide carriage 50, through the key 52, and through the band to below the slab.

Clamping shoe 60: a small horizontal block below the slab and directly under the band, drawn in section with hatching, its flat top surface against the lower face 14 and extending past the band to left and right so that the block spans the band. The lower end of the stem of the clamp knob 58 is received in the block.

12 upper face
14 lower face

# FIG. 1

## View
Perspective view of the assembled drilling jig resting on a workpiece, seen from above and slightly to one side, so that the top of the jig and the near edge of the panel are both visible. Plain black outline on white, all line work well inside the drawing area.

## Structures and relationships

Workpiece 90: a flat rectangular panel in perspective, front face upward, occupying most of the drawing area and drawn as a thin slab so its thickness shows along the near side. Its straight near-side boundary is the workpiece edge 92.

Rail 10: a long straight bar of rectangular cross section lying flat on the front face of the panel, running from the near edge inward across the panel at a right angle to the workpiece edge 92 and stopping short of the far boundary of the panel. Its flat underside contacts the front face along its length.

Longitudinal slot 16: a narrow straight opening through the bar, running lengthwise along the middle of the bar's top face with rounded ends, stopping short of both ends of the bar.

Distance marks 18: a row of short evenly spaced transverse strokes on the top face, running parallel to the longitudinal slot 16 along one side of it for most of the bar's length. The strokes carry no text.

Fence 30: shown schematically as a flat plate lying across the top of the bar at the end nearest the panel edge, standing out past one long side of the bar. A flange descends from that outstanding part, passes below the level of the bar's underside, and stands against the near-side thickness of the panel. Two small round fastener heads are drawn on the plate.

First guide carriage 50 and second guide carriage 70: two separate rectangular blocks seated on the top face of the bar and spaced apart along it, the first guide carriage 50 the nearer of the two to the fence 30 and the second guide carriage 70 the farther. No bar, link, or arm joins them. Each block spans the width of the bar, sits over the longitudinal slot 16, and carries on its top a round knurled head and, spaced from that head along the bar, the open top of a short vertical sleeve.

The end of the bar remote from the fence 30 has a shallow V-shaped indentation in its outer end edge, opening away from the fence, shown schematically.

## View
Top plan view of the drilling jig lying on a panel, seen square on from directly above. Plain black outline on white, all line work well inside the drawing area.

## Structures and relationships

A large rectangle drawn in outline represents the panel beneath the jig, shown schematically. Its left boundary is the straight edge the jig is referenced from.

Rail 10: a long narrow rectangle lying horizontally, its left end at the left boundary of the panel rectangle and its right end short of the right boundary, its long axis perpendicular to that left boundary.

At the left end, a plate is drawn across the bar and standing out past the lower long side of the bar, shown schematically, carrying two small circles for fastener heads.

A narrow lengthwise opening with rounded ends runs along the long centerline of the bar, stopping short of both ends.

Distance marks 18: a row of short evenly spaced strokes just above the lengthwise opening and parallel to it, running along most of the bar. No text.

Transverse center index 24: a single mark crossing the bar at the midpoint of its length, perpendicular to the long axis, drawn on the bar material on both sides of the lengthwise opening and reaching both long sides. It is longer and heavier than the strokes of the distance marks 18.

Two rectangular blocks are seated on the bar over the lengthwise opening, spaced apart along the bar, each spanning the width of the bar, shown schematically. The left block lies between the plate and the transverse center index 24; the right block lies between the transverse center index 24 and the right end. Each block shows two circles on the long centerline, spaced apart along it: a plain circle for the opening of a vertical sleeve, which is the left-hand circle, and a scalloped-rim circle for a knurled head, which is the right-hand circle.

First pointer 62: a short tapered index projecting from the upper long side of the left block toward the distance marks 18, its tip just clear of the strokes and on the same transverse line as the center of the plain circle of that block.

Second pointer 82: a short tapered index of the same form on the right block, projecting toward the distance marks 18, its tip just clear of the strokes and on the same transverse line as the center of the plain circle of that block.

Sight notch 26: a shallow V-shaped indentation cut into the right end edge of the bar, opening through that end edge, its apex on the long centerline and pointing back toward the interior of the bar.

Centerline 94: a short straight line on the panel within the opening of the sight notch 26, lying on the long centerline of the bar. It is drawn nowhere else, the bar covering it elsewhere.

## Cutting plane for FIG. 3
A broken cutting-plane line lies on the long centerline of the bar, parallel to its long axis. Its left end segment begins in the open panel area left of the left end of the bar; its right end segment ends on the bar between the right block and the sight notch 26; the two end segments are separated by a gap. An arrow at each end points perpendicular to the line toward the lower boundary of the drawing area, and the designation 3 is placed at both ends, giving line 3-3.

# FIG. 2

## View
Top plan view of the drilling jig lying on a panel, seen square on from above. Plain black outline on white, all line work well inside the drawing area.

## Structures and relationships

A large outline rectangle is the panel beneath the jig, shown schematically; its left boundary is the straight edge the jig is referenced from.

Rail 10: a long narrow horizontal rectangle, its left end at the left boundary of the panel rectangle, its right end short of the right boundary, its long axis perpendicular to that left boundary. A narrow lengthwise opening with rounded ends runs along the long centerline of the bar, stopping short of both ends. At the left end a plate crosses the bar and stands out past its lower long side, shown schematically, with two small circles for fastener heads.

Distance marks 18: a row of short evenly spaced strokes just above that opening and parallel to it, along most of the bar. No text.

Transverse center index 24: one mark crossing the bar at the midpoint of its length, perpendicular to the long axis, on the bar material both sides of the opening and reaching both long sides, longer and heavier than the strokes of the distance marks 18.

Two rectangular blocks sit on the bar over the opening, spaced apart along it and each spanning its width, shown schematically. The left block lies between the plate and the transverse center index 24, the right block between that index and the right end. Each block shows two circles on the long centerline, spaced apart along it: a plain circle for a vertical sleeve opening, the left-hand circle, and a scalloped-rim circle for a knurled head, the right-hand circle.

First pointer 62: a short tapered index from the upper long side of the left block reaching toward the distance marks 18, its tip just clear of the strokes and on the same transverse line as the center of the plain circle of that block.

Second pointer 82: an index of the same form on the right block, its tip just clear of the strokes and on the same transverse line as the center of the plain circle of that block.

Sight notch 26: a shallow V-shaped indentation in the right end edge of the bar, opening through that edge, its apex on the long centerline and pointing back into the bar.

Centerline 94: a short straight line on the panel inside the opening of the sight notch 26, on the long centerline of the bar, drawn nowhere else because the bar covers it elsewhere.

## Cutting plane for FIG. 3
A broken cutting-plane line lies on the long centerline of the bar, parallel to its long axis. Its left end segment begins in open panel area left of the left end of the bar; its right end segment ends on the bar between the right block and the sight notch 26; a gap separates the two segments. An arrow at each end points perpendicular to the line toward the lower boundary of the drawing area, and the designation 3 is placed at both ends, giving line 3-3.

10 rail

94 centerline

10 targets the bar between the plate and the left block. 18 targets the strokes well inside the run. 24 targets the transverse mark. 26 targets the V indentation. 62 targets the index on the left block. 82 targets the index on the right block. 94 targets the line inside the notch opening.
